newsitem.title: Belgium: Key sex charges against Belgium's Di Rupo dropped.
newsitem.headline: Key sex charges against Belgium's Di Rupo dropped.

text.p: Belgium's highest court has concluded that the main allegations against Deputy Prime Minister Elio Di Rupo of having sex with under-age boys are baseless, the parliament president said on Monday.

But francophone regional government minister Jean-Pierre Grafe -- also alleged to have had sex with people under the legal age of consent of 16 -- told Belga news agency he was innocent but felt obliged to resign.

The Cour de Cassation, due to hand over a report on Grafe on Tuesday, on Monday handed a special parliamentary commission a report of its investigations into two files of allegations against Di Rupo -- one based on a single witness and another based on anonymous sources.
"According to the report, no credibility can be accorded to the sole witness," parliament president Raymond Langendries told reporters during a break in the meeting of the commission.

"There is not the slightest serious indication that could warrant the indictment of Deputy Prime Minister Di Rupo before the Cour de Cassation," he added, referring to the first of the two case files against the number two in the Belgian government.
Di Rupo has consistently denied the allegations against him, and Belgian media questioned the reliability of Olivier Trugsnach, the sole identified witness.

But they have nevertheless served to undermine public confidence in Belgium's political and legal system, already weakened by the country's unrelated child sex abuse and murder scandal and ensuing revelations of bungling by investigators.
However, the commission decided to continue work on the second set of anonymous allegations against Di Rupo.
Whatever it decides -- to reject the allegations, to uphold them and indict Di Rupo or to ask for more investigations -- must then go to the full parliament to be put to the vote.
Langendries said the commission has called in the Brussels public prosecutor who compiled the case files on Di Rupo.
The court's damning report on the Trugsnach-based file is a slap in the face for the prosecutor and the police for failing to fully investigate the allegations before airing them.

The Di Rupo affair has been another nail in the coffin of Belgian public confidence that has been shaken since the arrest in mid-August of rapist Marc Dutroux, the subsequent rescue of two young girls and discovery of the bodies of four more.
Revelations of police and judicial bungling in earlier investigations in the hunt for missing children have further fuelled public anger and disgust.

In October more than 250,000 people took to the streets of Brussels in support of the victims and their families in a demonstration that crossed the country's language divide and rapidly turned into a show of anger at the system.
The government has rushed through a series of legal reforms and the leaders of the main political parties on Saturday began a process that should lead to long-awaited political changes.
But that still may be too late for Di Rupo, even if parliament decides he has no case to answer.
An indictment would mean sending Di Rupo to the Cour de Cassation for a full investigation, a move that would end his political career.

A similar procedure brought down former NATO Secretary General Willy Claes, who was forced to resign in October 1995 after parliament indicted him over allegations of bribery when he was a Belgian economics minister in the late eighties.

Even if parliament decides the charges against Di Rupo are unfounded, some of his peers have already called for his resignation on the grounds that a publicly-known homosexual should not hold high government office.
